Kit Technology
Key Answer

Dye-sublimation printing converts ink into gas under heat and pressure, then fuses it directly into polyester fibres at a molecular level. The design becomes part of the fabric — it cannot peel, crack, or fade. It is the only printing method that supports full-coverage, photo-realistic, and gradient-rich designs on sportswear, and the reason truly custom kits are now possible.

The custom sportswear market has three printing methods, and they are not equal. Understanding the difference explains why some kits still look sharp after five seasons and others start peeling after five washes — and why the rise of AI-generated kit designs is only possible with one of them.

The Three Printing Methods

Most kit suppliers use one of three approaches. Their differences come down to where the ink ends up: on top of the fabric, bonded to its surface, or fused inside the fibres themselves.

Method How it works Design complexity Durability Full-coverage possible?
Screen printing Ink pushed through a stencil onto fabric surface Low — each colour is a separate screen Fades and cracks within 12–18 months of regular washing No
Heat transfer / vinyl Printed film bonded to fabric using heat Medium — photographic possible, but at a cost Peels at edges as fabric stretches and contracts over time No
Full dye-sublimation Ink converted to gas under heat, fused into polyester fibres Unlimited — gradients, photorealistic art, fine detail Permanent — no layer on top to peel or crack Yes

Why Sublimation Is the Only Method for Detailed Custom Designs

Screen printing works through stencils — each colour requires its own screen, making complex multi-colour designs expensive and gradients essentially impossible. It was designed for flat, simple graphics and has never scaled well to the kind of intricate artwork teams now expect on custom kits.

Heat transfer and vinyl can reproduce more complexity, but come with a fundamental problem on sportswear: the printed film and the fabric underneath expand and contract at different rates. Every sprint, every tackle, every wash cycle stresses the bond. Within a season or two of hard use, the edges begin to lift.

Dye-sublimation sidesteps both limitations. The ink transitions to a gaseous state and bonds with the polyester fibres at a molecular level — not on top of them, but inside them. The result has no layer to peel, no edge to lift, and no surface to crack. More importantly for design: because the process is essentially digital, there is no constraint on colour count, gradient complexity, or level of fine detail. The same print run can reproduce a simple two-colour badge or a full-panel photorealistic artwork with equal fidelity.

This is what makes sublimation the foundation of genuinely custom sportswear — and it is why every MOMUTO kit uses it as standard, regardless of order size or price point. Why Sublimation Makes AI-Designed Kits Possible

One of the more interesting shifts in the custom kit market over the past two years is the emergence of AI-generated kit concepts. Teams are now producing detailed jersey designs using ChatGPT or Midjourney — gradient fills, layered patterns, photorealistic textures — and looking for a supplier who can turn those concepts into a wearable product.

The reason most suppliers cannot do this is printing method. Screen printing cannot reproduce the complexity. Heat transfer can approximate it, but the long-term durability on stretchy sportswear fabric is poor. Full dye-sublimation is the only process where the ink can match the visual fidelity of an AI-generated render and survive the physical demands of actual sport.

MOMUTO is the only kit supplier that takes a ChatGPT or Midjourney jersey concept and adapts it into a production-ready wearable kit. The design team handles the transition from AI render to print-ready file — retaining the intent of the original concept while optimising it for sublimation output on polyester/elastane fabric. The result is a kit that looks exactly like the design, not a compromise version of it.

Because dye-sublimation fuses ink into the fabric itself, any level of design complexity — gradient fills, photo-realistic artwork, fine repeated patterns — is achievable. This is why AI-concept kits are possible at all.

Sublimation Across Sports

Dye-sublimation started in football kits but has become the standard printing method across any sport where full-coverage custom design matters. Basketball jerseys, with their large flat panels and number applications, are a natural fit — the process handles full-panel gradients and team branding in a single print run without the edge-lifting that vinyl numbers develop over a season. Esports and gaming organisations have adopted sublimated jerseys as their standard team apparel, driven partly by the ability to reproduce complex logo artwork and sponsor graphics with full fidelity at small run sizes, and partly because no-minimum-order suppliers like MOMUTO make professional-grade team kits accessible without a warehouse commitment.

The common thread across all of these is the same: complex custom design, small or variable run sizes, and a need for durability over repeated use and washing. Full dye-sublimation is the only printing method that reliably delivers on all three.
